title: Glaucoma, Cataract and Retinal Disease
summary: Learn the major chronic causes of vision loss and how they are detected and treated.

lessons.title: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma and Optic Nerve Cupping

levels.kid:
Inside your eye is a clear fluid that is always flowing in and draining out, like water in a sink with the tap on. If the drain gets slow, pressure can build up inside the eye.

At the back of the eye is the **optic nerve**, a cable that carries pictures to your brain. In **glaucoma**, this cable slowly gets damaged, often when the pressure is too high for that eye.

The tricky part is that it doesn't hurt. Vision fades from the edges first, so people don't notice. That's why eye doctors look at the nerve and check the eye pressure. Eye drops can help the fluid drain or slow how much is made. They protect the vision that is left.
levels.hs:
**Glaucoma** is a group of diseases in which the **optic nerve** is slowly damaged, causing permanent loss of vision. It is a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. The most common form in Europe and the Americas is **primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG)**.

The front of the eye is filled with **aqueous humor**, a fluid made by the ciliary body. It drains out through the **trabecular meshwork**, a sponge-like filter in the **drainage angle** where the iris meets the cornea. In POAG the angle looks open, but outflow through the meshwork is reduced. This can raise **intraocular pressure (IOP)**. Normal IOP is roughly 10 to 21 mmHg.

Raised pressure, plus other factors, kills **retinal ganglion cells**, whose fibers form the optic nerve. When doctors look at the optic disc, they see the central pit, called the **cup**, getting bigger. This is **optic nerve cupping**.

POAG is painless and affects side (peripheral) vision first, so many people don't know they have it until the damage is advanced. Risk factors include age, family history, African ancestry, and high IOP.

Example: a 60-year-old at a routine eye check has an IOP of 26 mmHg and enlarged cups. A visual field test shows early peripheral loss. Daily pressure-lowering eye drops can slow further damage, but the vision already lost does not come back.
levels.college:
**Primary open-angle glaucoma** is a chronic, progressive **optic neuropathy** with characteristic optic disc changes and matching visual field loss. The drainage angle is open on **gonioscopy**, and there is no secondary cause such as steroid use or pigment dispersion.

**Aqueous dynamics.** The ciliary body epithelium secretes aqueous at about 2.5 µL/min. Drainage follows two routes:
- **Conventional (trabecular) outflow**: through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal and the episcleral veins. Most resistance sits at the juxtacanalicular meshwork.
- **Uveoscleral outflow**: through the ciliary muscle.
In POAG, trabecular resistance rises and IOP increases. However, IOP is a risk factor, not part of the definition. **Normal-tension glaucoma** damages the nerve with IOP within the normal range, and many people with **ocular hypertension** never develop glaucoma.

**Structural signs:**
- Increased **cup-to-disc ratio** (a vertical ratio above about 0.6 is suspicious), or asymmetry of 0.2 or more between the two eyes
- Rim thinning that breaks the **ISNT rule** (normal rim width: inferior ≥ superior ≥ nasal ≥ temporal)
- Disc hemorrhages, notching, and retinal nerve fiber layer defects, often measured with **OCT**

**Functional signs.** The arcuate pattern of nerve fibers produces **nasal steps**, **arcuate scotomas** and paracentral defects. These are tracked with automated perimetry. Central vision is often spared until late.

**Treatment** lowers IOP, the only proven modifiable factor:
- **Prostaglandin analogues** (latanoprost) increase uveoscleral outflow and are first line.
- **Beta-blockers** (timolol) and **carbonic anhydrase inhibitors** (dorzolamide) reduce aqueous production.
- **Alpha-2 agonists** (brimonidine) reduce production and increase outflow.
- **Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT)** improves meshwork outflow.
- Surgery: **trabeculectomy**, tube shunts, or minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS).
levels.phd:
POAG is a neurodegeneration of **retinal ganglion cells (RGCs)**. The main site of injury is the **lamina cribrosa**, a sieve-like plate of collagen through which RGC axons leave the eye. The mechanical forces on this plate depend on the **translaminar pressure gradient**, which is IOP minus retrolaminar (cerebrospinal fluid) pressure. Studies by Berdahl and Ren found lower CSF pressure in normal-tension glaucoma, which supports the gradient model.

**Mechanisms of axon injury:**
- **Biomechanical**: the lamina deforms and remodels, pushing backward (posterior bowing). This compresses axons and blocks **axoplasmic transport**. Quigley's classic primate experiments showed that transport stalls at the lamina when IOP is raised.
- **Vascular**: unstable perfusion matters. Low ocular perfusion pressure and nocturnal hypotension are risk factors.
- **Glial and immune**: reactive astrocytes, complement activation (C1q tags synapses early) and loss of neurotrophin supply, especially reduced retrograde BDNF signalling.
- **Mitochondrial and metabolic**: NAD+ decline. Williams and colleagues showed that nicotinamide prevents glaucoma in DBA/2J mice.
RGCs then die by apoptosis, with axon degeneration involving SARM1.

**Trabecular pathology.** Outflow resistance rises from extracellular matrix buildup, cell loss and increased tissue stiffness, partly driven by TGF-β2. Genetics: **MYOC (TIGR)** mutations cause juvenile open-angle glaucoma through misfolded myocilin and ER stress in meshwork cells. **OPTN** and **TBK1** are linked to normal-tension glaucoma. Genome-wide studies (CAV1/CAV2, TMCO1, CDKN2B-AS1) implicate many common variants, enabling polygenic risk scores.

**Landmark trials:**
- **OHTS**: treating ocular hypertension lowered 5-year conversion from 9.5% to 4.4%. Thin central corneal thickness was an independent risk factor.
- **EMGT**: each 1 mmHg reduction in IOP lowered the risk of progression by about 10%.
- **CNTGS**: lowering IOP by 30% slowed normal-tension glaucoma.
- **UKGTS**: latanoprost preserved visual fields compared with placebo.
Structural loss often comes before detectable field loss. An estimated 25 to 35% of RGCs may be lost before standard perimetry shows defects.
levels.expert:
Clinical practice centres on a **target IOP**: a range set for each patient from the baseline pressure, stage of damage, rate of progression and life expectancy. Clinicians often aim for a 20 to 30% reduction at first, then revise based on how fast the disease is changing. Progression is judged by **trend analysis** (visual field index slope, guided progression analysis). Rates faster than about -1 to -2 dB per year in a young patient threaten lifetime vision.

**Pitfalls:**
- **Corneal thickness and biomechanics** distort Goldmann readings. Thin or low-hysteresis corneas underestimate true risk, and thin corneas after refractive surgery give falsely low readings.
- **OCT 'red disease'**: myopic discs, tilted discs and peripapillary atrophy fall outside normative databases. **Floor effects** limit retinal nerve fiber layer OCT in advanced disease, where macular ganglion cell analysis and 10-2 fields work better.
- **Glaucoma mimics**: compressive lesions such as pituitary tumours and anterior visual pathway meningiomas can cause cupping. Pallor that is worse than the cupping, vertically aligned field defects, young age or a falling visual acuity call for neuroimaging. This is an important link to neurosurgery.
- **Adherence**: up to half of patients use drops inconsistently. Daily IOP fluctuation and peaks at night are missed in clinic.

**Recent advances:**
- The **LiGHT trial** found SLT as first-line treatment non-inferior to drops, with fewer patients needing surgery. Many centres now offer laser first.
- **Rho-kinase inhibitors** (netarsudil) act directly on the trabecular meshwork, and **latanoprostene bunod** releases nitric oxide.
- **Sustained-release implants**, such as the bimatoprost intracameral implant and travoprost implants, help with adherence.
- **MIGS** devices (iStent, Hydrus) are suited to mild-to-moderate disease, often combined with cataract surgery.

**Open questions:** neuroprotection without lowering IOP. Brimonidine showed a signal in the LoGTS trial but had confounded dropout. Nicotinamide/pyruvate trials are under way. Other open areas include RGC replacement and axon regeneration (for example PTEN/SOCS3 deletion in models), home tonometry, 24-hour IOP sensors, and AI interpretation of disc photos for screening.

keyPoints: POAG is a chronic optic neuropathy with an open drainage angle
Reduced trabecular outflow raises IOP, a major modifiable risk factor
Cupping: enlarged cup-to-disc ratio and rim thinning breaking ISNT
Peripheral field loss is painless, so screening matters
Treatment lowers IOP: prostaglandin drops, laser trabeculoplasty, surgery
Normal-tension glaucoma shows IOP is not the whole story

test.q: Which structure mainly drains aqueous humor in conventional outflow?
test.explain: Aqueous leaves through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal. The ciliary body makes aqueous rather than draining it.

test.q: Which part of vision is usually lost first in POAG?
test.explain: Arcuate and peripheral defects come first. Central vision is often spared until late, which is why the disease goes unnoticed.

test.q: What does 'open-angle' mean in POAG?
choices: The optic cup has opened fully
test.explain: On gonioscopy the drainage angle is open, but outflow through the meshwork is still reduced.

test.q: Which finding suggests glaucomatous cupping?
choices: Small cup with a pink, healthy rim
test.explain: A large vertical cup-to-disc ratio means the neural rim has been lost. A thick inferior rim is normal under the ISNT rule.

test.q: How do prostaglandin analogues such as latanoprost lower IOP?
test.explain: Prostaglandin analogues increase uveoscleral outflow. Beta-blockers are the drugs that reduce aqueous production.

test.q: Normal-tension glaucoma shows that:
choices: High IOP is required for nerve damage
Glaucoma is a disease of the lens
IOP is a risk factor, not the definition
test.explain: The optic nerve can be damaged even when IOP is in the normal range. Glaucoma is defined by the neuropathy, not by the pressure.

test.q: Timolol lowers IOP mainly by:
test.explain: Beta-blockers reduce how much aqueous the ciliary body secretes.

test.q: Which is a recognised risk factor for POAG?
test.explain: Age, family history, African ancestry and high IOP raise risk. A thin cornea, not a thick one, is a risk factor.

test.q: Which test images the retinal nerve fiber layer?
test.explain: OCT measures the thickness of the nerve fiber layer. Tonometry measures pressure, and gonioscopy examines the angle.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for the pressure inside the eye?
test.explain: IOP stands for intraocular pressure. Normal is roughly 10 to 21 mmHg.

test.q: The ___ rule states the normal rim is thickest inferiorly, then superior, nasal and temporal.
test.explain: ISNT stands for inferior ≥ superior ≥ nasal ≥ temporal. Breaking this pattern suggests glaucoma.

test.q: The clear fluid filling the front of the eye is called aqueous ___.
test.explain: Aqueous humor is made by the ciliary body and drains through the angle.

kidTest.q: What does the optic nerve do?
kidTest.explain: The optic nerve is the cable from the eye to the brain.

kidTest.q: Why don't people notice glaucoma early?
kidTest.explain: It is painless and starts at the edges of vision.

kidTest.q: What can build up when the eye's drain is slow?
kidTest.explain: Fluid keeps coming in, so pressure rises.

kidTest.q: How do doctors often treat glaucoma?
kidTest.explain: Drops help fluid drain or reduce how much is made.

kidTest.q: The eye disease that harms the optic nerve: g _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Glaucoma slowly damages the optic nerve.

advancedTest.q: A patient with normal-tension glaucoma has low CSF pressure. Which model best explains the nerve damage?
advancedTest.explain: IOP minus CSF pressure determines strain on the lamina. Low CSF pressure raises this gradient even when IOP is normal.

advancedTest.q: A patient's OCT shows retinal nerve fiber thinning, but standard perimetry is normal. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Structural loss can precede field loss
The disc is likely a congenital variant
Visual field tests are more sensitive
The OCT result is likely artefact
advancedTest.explain: A substantial share of ganglion cells can be lost before standard perimetry shows a defect.

advancedTest.q: A 45-year-old has cupping, disc pallor exceeding the cupping, and a vertically aligned field defect. What is the best next step?
advancedTest.explain: Pallor greater than cupping and vertically aligned defects suggest a compressive lesion that mimics glaucoma, so imaging is needed.

advancedTest.q: EMGT found about a 10% lower progression risk per mmHg of IOP lowered. What does this mainly support?
choices: Aiming for a fixed IOP of 21 mmHg
advancedTest.explain: A graded benefit per mmHg supports individual target pressures based on stage and rate of progression, not a single cutoff.

lessons.title: Cataract: Causes and Lens Replacement Surgery

levels.kid:
Inside your eye there is a tiny clear lens, about the size of a lentil. It bends light so pictures land sharply at the back of your eye, like a camera lens.

When people get old, that lens can slowly turn cloudy and yellow, like a window getting foggy. This is called a **cataract**. Things look blurry, colors look dull, and bright lights seem to glow.

The good news is that doctors can fix it! In a short operation, the surgeon makes a very tiny cut, breaks up the cloudy lens, and gently removes it. Then they slip in a new clear plastic lens that unfolds inside the eye. Many people see better the very next day.
levels.hs:
The **lens** sits behind the iris. It is a clear, flexible disc made of tightly packed cells filled with special proteins called **crystallins**. A **cataract** is any clouding of the lens. It is the leading cause of blindness worldwide, and most of that blindness could be treated with surgery.

Causes include:
- **Aging**, by far the most common cause. Lens proteins slowly become damaged and clump together.
- **Diabetes**, which speeds up lens changes.
- **Steroid medicines** taken over a long time.
- **UV sunlight** exposure and **smoking**.
- **Eye injury**, and **congenital** cataracts present at birth.

Symptoms come on gradually. People notice painless blurring, glare and halos around headlights at night, and faded colors. Some find their reading improves for a while ('second sight') because the lens starts focusing light more strongly.

Doctors see the cataract with a **slit lamp**. The red reflex, the orange glow you see in flash photos, looks dim or patchy.

There are no eye drops that reverse a cataract. The treatment is surgery: the cloudy lens is removed and replaced with an artificial **intraocular lens (IOL)**. Example: a 72-year-old who can no longer drive at night because of glare has surgery on one eye. Within days, she can read road signs clearly again.
levels.college:
The lens is avascular and keeps adding fiber cells throughout life, so its oldest cells sit in the center (the **nucleus**). Transparency depends on the orderly packing of α-, β- and γ-crystallins and on low light scatter. When proteins oxidize, cross-link and aggregate, light scatters and the lens becomes opaque.

**Morphologic types:**
- **Nuclear sclerotic**: the central lens hardens and turns yellow-brown with age. Its higher refractive power causes a **myopic shift**.
- **Cortical**: wedge-shaped 'spoke' opacities in the outer lens, linked to UV exposure and diabetes. They cause glare.
- **Posterior subcapsular (PSC)**: a plaque just in front of the back capsule. It is typical of corticosteroid use, diabetes and radiation, often appears in younger patients, and hurts reading and vision in bright light.

**Other causes:** galactosemia (galactitol builds up and draws in water), congenital rubella, trauma, uveitis, myotonic dystrophy ('Christmas tree' cataract), Wilson disease (sunflower cataract) and prior vitrectomy.

**When to operate:** surgery is indicated when vision loss interferes with daily life, not at a fixed acuity cutoff.

**Phacoemulsification** is the standard technique:
- A self-sealing corneal incision of about 2-2.8 mm is made.
- Viscoelastic gel protects the cornea and holds the anterior chamber open.
- **Capsulorhexis**: a continuous circular tear is made in the anterior capsule.
- Hydrodissection frees the lens contents from the capsule.
- An ultrasonic probe breaks up and aspirates the nucleus, then the cortex is removed.
- A foldable acrylic IOL is placed inside the capsular bag.

Preoperative **biometry** (axial length plus corneal curvature) is used to calculate IOL power. Most patients recover within days, and serious complications are uncommon.
levels.phd:
Lens transparency rests on a short-range order of densely packed crystallins, which reach the highest protein concentration of any tissue in the body in the nucleus. Mature fiber cells have no organelles and carry out essentially no protein turnover, so the lens nucleus contains some of the oldest proteins in the body. α-Crystallin (αA/αB, encoded by CRYAA/CRYAB) acts as a small heat-shock-like chaperone that binds unfolding β/γ-crystallins. As its capacity runs out with age, high-molecular-weight aggregates form and scatter light.

The main pathways of protein damage include:
- **Oxidation**: glutathione falls, especially in the nucleus, because a barrier slows diffusion from the cortex. Methionine and cysteine residues oxidize and form disulfide cross-links.
- **Post-translational damage**: deamidation, racemization, truncation and glycation, including advanced glycation end-products in diabetes.
- **Photo-oxidation**: UV-B and tryptophan metabolites (kynurenines) produce yellow pigmentation.
- **The polyol pathway**: aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, or galactose to galactitol. These sugar alcohols cannot leave the cell, so they cause osmotic swelling. This explains galactosemic cataract and some acute diabetic cataracts.

Numerous mutations in crystallin, connexin (GJA3, GJA8) and other lens genes underlie the hereditary congenital cataracts.

Epidemiology from the Beaver Dam Eye Study and others links cortical cataract to UV exposure, and PSC to corticosteroids. In AREDS, antioxidant supplements did not prevent cataract progression. Pharmacologic reversal remains unproven: lanosterol dissolved aggregates in a 2015 *Nature* study, but later work failed to reproduce clear human benefit.

Surgery has evolved from couching, to intracapsular extraction, to extracapsular extraction. Ridley implanted the first IOL in 1949, after observing that PMMA canopy fragments were tolerated in the eyes of injured RAF pilots. Kelman then introduced phacoemulsification in 1967.

Modern IOL power formulas (SRK/T, Haigis, Barrett Universal II, and ray-tracing or AI formulas) predict the refractive outcome within ±0.5 D in roughly 80% of eyes. Key error sources are axial length and the predicted effective lens position.

The main long-term complication is **posterior capsule opacification (PCO)**, in which residual lens epithelial cells migrate and transdifferentiate. Square-edged optic designs reduce it, and Nd:YAG capsulotomy treats it.
levels.expert:
**Preoperative assessment**

The real work is matching the operation to the eye. Key pitfalls:
- **Biometry after refractive surgery**: previous LASIK invalidates the standard keratometry assumptions. Without dedicated formulas such as Barrett True-K, the result is a hyperopic surprise.
- **Tamsulosin and other α1A antagonists**: these cause **intraoperative floppy iris syndrome**. The iris billows, prolapses through incisions and constricts. Risk persists even after the drug is stopped, so management relies on iris hooks or rings, intracameral phenylephrine/ketorolac and low-flow settings.
- **Pseudoexfoliation**: weak zonules raise the risk of lens dislocation. Capsular tension rings may be needed.
- **Ocular comorbidity**: always check the macula and optic nerve before promising an outcome. OCT can reveal epiretinal membrane or early macular disease.

**IOL choice is now a refractive decision**
- **Toric IOLs** correct corneal astigmatism, but every 1° of rotation costs about 3% of their effect.
- **Multifocal and trifocal IOLs** reduce dependence on spectacles, at the price of halos and reduced contrast.
- **Extended-depth-of-focus** designs balance these trade-offs.
- **Light-adjustable lenses** can be tuned with UV light after surgery.
- Patients with macular disease are poor candidates for diffractive optics.

**Complications to know**
- **Posterior capsule rupture with vitreous loss**: this raises the risk of retinal detachment, cystoid macular edema and retained lens fragments.
- **Endophthalmitis**: rare. The ESCRS study showed that intracameral cefuroxime reduced it roughly fivefold, and intracameral antibiotics are now widely used outside the US.
- **Toxic anterior segment syndrome**: a sterile, early inflammation, distinguished from infection by its timing and lack of pain.
- **Pseudophakic CME (Irvine-Gass syndrome)**: peaks at around 4-6 weeks.

**Advances and open questions**

Femtosecond laser-assisted surgery creates precise capsulotomies, but the FEMCAT and FACT trials found no clear outcome advantage over manual phaco, at higher cost. Immediate sequential bilateral surgery is gaining acceptance where strict asepsis between eyes is maintained.

Globally, manual small-incision cataract surgery (MSICS) delivers comparable outcomes at very low cost. Organizations such as Aravind in India have scaled it to enormous volumes.

Open questions include accommodating IOLs that truly restore near focus, drug therapies that prevent opacification, and preventing pediatric aphakic glaucoma after congenital cataract surgery. In infants, early surgery prevents deprivation amblyopia.

keyPoints: A cataract is clouding of the normally clear lens
Aging is the main cause; diabetes, steroids, UV, smoking and trauma add risk
Types: nuclear sclerotic, cortical, posterior subcapsular
Symptoms: painless gradual blur, glare, halos, faded colors
Treatment is surgery: phacoemulsification plus an intraocular lens
Posterior capsule opacification is common later and treated with YAG laser

test.q: What is a cataract?
test.explain: A cataract is any opacity of the lens. Raised pressure describes glaucoma, a different disease.

test.q: Which is by far the most common cause of cataract?
test.explain: Age-related protein damage causes most cataracts. The other options are real causes, but much rarer.

test.q: Long-term corticosteroid use is classically linked to which cataract type?
test.explain: Steroids typically cause posterior subcapsular cataract. Sunflower cataract is linked to Wilson disease.

test.q: A nuclear sclerotic cataract often makes the eye more:
test.explain: The hardened nucleus bends light more strongly, causing a myopic shift. This is why some patients briefly read better without glasses.

test.q: What is the standard modern cataract operation?
test.explain: Phacoemulsification uses ultrasound to break up and remove the lens. Trabeculectomy is a glaucoma operation.

test.q: What replaces the removed natural lens?
test.explain: A foldable artificial intraocular lens (IOL) is placed in the capsular bag.

test.q: Which symptom is typical of cataract?
test.explain: Cataracts cause gradual, painless blur with glare and halos. A curtain over the vision suggests retinal detachment.

test.q: Months after surgery, vision blurs again because the capsule behind the IOL has clouded. The treatment is:
test.explain: Posterior capsule opacification is cleared by making an opening in the capsule with an Nd:YAG laser.

test.q: When is cataract surgery usually recommended?
test.explain: Surgery is based on how much the patient's daily function is affected, not on a fixed cutoff. No drops reverse cataract.

test.q: The clear proteins packed inside lens fibers are called ___.
test.explain: Orderly packing of crystallins keeps the lens transparent.

test.q: What is the name of the circular opening made in the front of the lens capsule during phaco?
test.explain: A continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis opens the capsule while leaving a strong rim to hold the IOL.

test.q: Measuring axial length and corneal curvature to choose IOL power is called ___.
test.explain: Biometry feeds formulas that calculate the power of IOL needed.

kidTest.q: What is a cataract?
choices: A cloudy lens in the eye
A tear in the eye's skin
kidTest.explain: The clear lens becomes cloudy, like a foggy window.

kidTest.q: Who usually gets cataracts?
kidTest.explain: Most cataracts come with getting older.

kidTest.q: How do things look through a cataract?
kidTest.explain: Cloudy lenses make things blurry with faded colors.

kidTest.q: How do doctors fix a cataract?
choices: Put in a new clear lens
kidTest.explain: The cloudy lens is removed and replaced with a new clear one.

kidTest.q: The clear part inside the eye that turns cloudy is the l _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The lens focuses light, and a cataract makes it cloudy.

advancedTest.q: Why does galactosemia cause cataract in infants?
choices: Galactose blocks UV filtering by kynurenine pigments
Galactitol is trapped in lens cells and draws in water
advancedTest.explain: Aldose reductase turns galactose into galactitol, which cannot leave lens cells and causes osmotic swelling. Transdifferentiation describes posterior capsule opacification, not this.

advancedTest.q: Why does the lens nucleus accumulate damaged protein so heavily with age?
choices: Its cells divide rapidly and misfold newly made crystallins
Its blood supply delivers oxidants straight to the center
Its fibers lack organelles and essentially do not turn over protein
Its capsule actively pumps glutathione out of the nucleus
advancedTest.explain: Mature fibers have no organelles and no protein turnover, so damage builds up. The lens has no blood supply, and nuclear glutathione falls because of a diffusion barrier.

advancedTest.q: A post-LASIK patient has cataract surgery using standard keratometry and ends up farsighted. The most likely reason is:
choices: Tamsulosin caused floppy iris during the surgery
Posterior capsule opacification formed early on
Altered corneal shape breaks the formula assumptions
The femtosecond laser misplaced the capsulotomy
advancedTest.explain: After refractive surgery, standard keratometry misrepresents corneal power, so the chosen IOL is too weak and leaves a hyperopic surprise. Dedicated formulas avoid this.

advancedTest.q: Why would a patient with macular disease be steered away from a diffractive multifocal IOL?
choices: It rotates easily and loses astigmatic correction
It prevents later Nd:YAG capsulotomy from working
Its optics reduce contrast that a weak macula needs
It raises the risk of endophthalmitis after surgery
advancedTest.explain: Diffractive optics split light and reduce contrast sensitivity, which harms an already compromised macula. Rotation is a problem for toric IOLs, not multifocal ones.

lessons.title: Diabetic Retinopathy and Macular Edema

levels.kid:
Inside the back of your eye is a thin layer called the **retina**. It works like the screen in a movie theater, catching pictures so your brain can see them. Tiny blood vessels bring it food and oxygen.

When someone has diabetes, there is too much sugar in their blood for a long time. That extra sugar slowly hurts those tiny vessels. They can leak like old garden hoses. Sometimes the eye grows new vessels, but they are weak and break easily.

If fluid leaks into the very center of the retina, things look blurry. That is called **macular edema**.

The good news: an eye doctor can spot problems early with a special eye check every year. Keeping blood sugar steady helps protect the eyes.
levels.hs:
**Diabetic retinopathy** is damage to the retina's small blood vessels caused by long-term high blood sugar. It is one of the leading causes of vision loss in working-age adults worldwide.

High glucose injures the walls of **capillaries**, the tiniest vessels. Two main problems follow:
- **Leakage**: weakened vessels bulge into tiny balloons called **microaneurysms** and leak blood, fluid and fats.
- **Blockage**: capillaries close off, so parts of the retina starve for oxygen (**ischemia**).

The disease has two stages:
- **Non-proliferative (NPDR)**: microaneurysms, dot-and-blot hemorrhages and yellow fatty **hard exudates**.
- **Proliferative (PDR)**: the oxygen-starved retina sends out a growth signal called **VEGF** (vascular endothelial growth factor). Fragile new vessels grow (**neovascularization**), which can bleed into the eye's gel or pull the retina loose.

**Diabetic macular edema (DME)** is swelling of the **macula**, the central retina used for reading and recognizing faces. It can occur at any stage and is the most common cause of vision loss in diabetes.

Early disease often causes no symptoms. That is why people with diabetes need regular dilated eye exams. Example: a 45-year-old with type 2 diabetes may see perfectly well while their exam already shows microaneurysms. Good control of blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol slows the damage.
levels.college:
**Pathogenesis.** Chronic hyperglycemia damages the retinal microvasculature through several pathways: the polyol pathway (aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol), formation of **advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)**, activation of protein kinase C, and oxidative stress. An early histologic sign is loss of **pericytes**, the contractile cells that support capillaries. Basement membrane thickening and endothelial dysfunction follow, and these lead to:
- **Increased permeability**: breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier causes edema and exudates.
- **Capillary non-perfusion**: ischemia upregulates **VEGF** through hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α).

**Classification (ETDRS-based)**
- **NPDR** (mild, moderate, severe): microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots (nerve fiber layer infarcts), venous beading and **IRMA** (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities). The **4-2-1 rule** defines severe NPDR: hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 or more, or IRMA in 1 or more.
- **PDR**: neovascularization of the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE). Complications include vitreous hemorrhage, **tractional retinal detachment** and neovascular glaucoma from new vessels on the iris (rubeosis).

**Diabetic macular edema** is graded as center-involving or non-center-involving. It is diagnosed and monitored with **optical coherence tomography (OCT)**, which measures retinal thickness and shows intraretinal fluid cysts.

**Detection and treatment**
- Screening uses dilated fundoscopy or retinal photography, including AI-graded systems.
- **Anti-VEGF intravitreal injections** (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab, faricimab) are first-line for center-involving DME.
- **Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP)** treats PDR. The laser ablates ischemic peripheral retina so it makes less VEGF.
- **Vitrectomy** treats non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage or traction.
- Intravitreal corticosteroids (dexamethasone or fluocinolone implants) are options when edema persists.

Risk rises with diabetes duration, poor glycemic control (HbA1c), hypertension, dyslipidemia, pregnancy and nephropathy.
levels.phd:
**Landmark trials** define the field. The **DCCT** (type 1) and **UKPDS** (type 2) showed that intensive glycemic control reduces the onset and progression of retinopathy. UKPDS also showed a benefit from tight blood pressure control. The DCCT/EDIC follow-up revealed **metabolic memory**: the benefit of earlier intensive control persisted for years after HbA1c levels converged. This is thought to reflect epigenetic changes and persistent AGE crosslinks.

**Early worsening** is a recognized paradox. Rapid HbA1c reduction, seen in the DCCT and more recently with semaglutide in SUSTAIN-6, can transiently worsen retinopathy, especially in eyes with pre-existing disease. Proposed mechanisms include a sudden drop in perfusion of ischemic retina and changes in IGF-1 and VEGF signaling.

**Molecular pathways** beyond VEGF-A matter. Angiopoietin-2 destabilizes pericyte-endothelial contacts by antagonizing Tie2. Faricimab, a bispecific antibody against both Ang-2 and VEGF-A, exploits this. Inflammation also contributes: leukostasis via ICAM-1, along with IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1. This explains the steroid responsiveness of some DME and why some eyes respond poorly to anti-VEGF. **Diabetic retinal neurodegeneration**, meaning thinning of the ganglion cell and inner plexiform layers and electroretinographic changes, can precede visible vasculopathy. This challenges a purely vascular model.

**Evidence base for therapy**
- The Diabetic Retinopathy Study (DRS) established that PRP roughly halves the risk of severe vision loss in high-risk PDR.
- ETDRS established focal and grid laser for clinically significant macular edema, which reduced moderate vision loss by about 50%.
- **DRCR Retina Network Protocol T** compared aflibercept, ranibizumab and bevacizumab for DME. Results were similar when baseline acuity was 20/40 or better. Aflibercept was superior at 1 year when acuity was 20/50 or worse, though this advantage narrowed by 2 years.
- **Protocol S** showed ranibizumab was non-inferior to PRP for PDR at 2 years, with less peripheral field loss and less vitrectomy. The PRP-versus-anti-VEGF debate continues.

Systemic factors such as fenofibrate (FIELD, ACCORD-Eye) slow progression independently of lipid lowering. The mechanism is unclear and may involve PPAR-α.
levels.expert:
**Choosing therapy around adherence.** Anti-VEGF treatment depends on regular injections. Real-world cohorts receive far fewer injections than trial patients and achieve smaller visual gains. Loss to follow-up is common in diabetic populations, and eyes with PDR treated with anti-VEGF alone have developed devastating neovascular glaucoma or tractional detachment after missed visits. Many retina specialists therefore combine PRP with anti-VEGF, or favor PRP, when follow-up is uncertain.

**Protocol V** found that eyes with center-involving DME and good acuity (20/25 or better) did similarly well with observation, laser, or anti-VEGF, provided treatment was started if vision dropped. Not every edema on OCT needs immediate injection.

**Protocol W and PANORAMA** showed that preventive anti-VEGF in severe NPDR reduced progression to PDR and center-involving DME. However, Protocol W showed no visual-acuity benefit at 4 years. This raises an open question: should we treat the anatomy or the patient?

**Imaging advances**
- **Ultra-widefield fluorescein angiography** shows predominantly peripheral lesions, which predict progression. Grading systems based only on the standard ETDRS fields may understage these eyes.
- **OCT angiography** quantifies foveal avascular zone enlargement and capillary dropout without dye, but it lacks leakage information.
- OCT biomarkers predict outcome: disorganization of retinal inner layers (**DRIL**), ellipsoid zone disruption and hyperreflective foci.

**Autonomous AI screening.** IDx-DR (now LumineticsCore) was the first FDA-authorized autonomous diagnostic AI in any medical field (2018). EyeArt followed. These systems extend screening into primary care, but ungradable images and performance across different populations remain concerns.

**Perioperative pitfalls**
- Cataract surgery can worsen DME. Pre-existing edema should be treated before surgery.
- In pregnancy, retinopathy may progress quickly, and anti-VEGF use is generally avoided.
- Preoperative anti-VEGF before vitrectomy for PDR reduces bleeding. It can also accelerate fibrovascular contraction (the **crunch phenomenon**), so timing matters.

**Frontiers** include longer-acting agents (high-dose aflibercept, the port delivery system), gene therapy that turns the eye into its own anti-VEGF factory, and attempts to target neurodegeneration directly.

keyPoints: Chronic hyperglycemia damages retinal capillaries, causing leakage and ischemia
NPDR shows microaneurysms, hemorrhages and exudates; PDR adds neovascularization
Retinal ischemia drives VEGF, which causes new vessel growth and edema
Diabetic macular edema is the most common cause of vision loss in diabetes and is tracked with OCT
Anti-VEGF injections treat DME; panretinal photocoagulation treats PDR
Early disease is silent, so regular dilated eye screening is essential

test.q: Which feature separates proliferative from non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
test.explain: New vessel growth defines PDR. The other three are signs of NPDR.

test.q: Which growth factor do ischemic retinal cells release to drive new vessel growth?
test.explain: Hypoxia raises HIF-1α, which upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).

test.q: Which imaging test is used to diagnose and monitor diabetic macular edema?
test.explain: OCT measures retinal thickness and shows intraretinal fluid.

test.q: What is the first-line treatment for center-involving diabetic macular edema?
test.explain: Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents are first-line. PRP is mainly used for proliferative disease.

test.q: How does panretinal photocoagulation help in PDR?
choices: It lowers pressure inside the eye
It seals each new vessel directly
It replaces the clouded natural lens
It ablates ischemic retina that makes VEGF
test.explain: Destroying oxygen-starved peripheral retina reduces the VEGF drive for neovascularization.

test.q: What is an early histologic sign of diabetic retinopathy?
test.explain: Pericyte dropout weakens capillaries and promotes microaneurysms.

test.q: Cotton-wool spots in diabetic retinopathy represent:
choices: Infarcts of the nerve fiber layer
test.explain: Cotton-wool spots are ischemic infarcts of the nerve fiber layer. Lipid deposits are hard exudates.

test.q: Why do people with diabetes need regular eye exams even when they see well?
choices: Eye drops are needed to slow the disease
Exams help to lower blood sugar levels
Vision loss appears first in childhood
Early retinopathy often has no symptoms
test.explain: Damage can be advanced before symptoms appear, so screening catches it early.

test.q: Which complication of PDR is caused by new vessels growing on the iris?
test.explain: Rubeosis (iris neovascularization) can block drainage and cause neovascular glaucoma.

test.q: Swelling of the central retina in diabetes is called diabetic macular ___.
test.explain: DME is fluid buildup in the macula.

test.q: What are the tiny outpouchings of weakened capillaries, the earliest visible sign of retinopathy, called?
test.explain: Microaneurysms are the first clinically visible lesion.

test.q: The 4-2-1 rule defines severe ___ (use the abbreviation).
test.explain: Severe NPDR means hemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, or IRMA in 1.

kidTest.q: What part of the eye works like a movie screen?
kidTest.explain: The retina catches pictures for the brain.

kidTest.q: What hurts the tiny eye vessels in diabetes?
kidTest.explain: High blood sugar over a long time damages the vessels.

kidTest.q: What can happen when fluid leaks into the center of the retina?
kidTest.explain: That swelling, called macular edema, blurs vision.

kidTest.q: How can a doctor find eye problems early?
kidTest.explain: Regular eye exams catch damage before it hurts vision.

kidTest.q: The weak new vessels can break and ___ easily. Hint: b _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: The fragile new vessels can break and bleed.

advancedTest.q: A patient with PDR is unlikely to return for follow-up. Which plan is most defensible?
choices: Oral fenofibrate as the sole therapy
Watchful waiting with a yearly photograph
advancedTest.explain: Anti-VEGF alone has failed badly when patients miss visits. PRP gives a durable effect.

advancedTest.q: After a rapid drop in HbA1c, a patient's retinopathy worsens. What best explains this?
choices: Development of resistance to anti-VEGF therapy
Metabolic memory of earlier poor control
Early worsening linked to perfusion and VEGF shifts
advancedTest.explain: Early worsening is a recognized transient effect of rapid glycemic improvement. Metabolic memory describes lasting benefit, not sudden decline.

advancedTest.q: What does targeting angiopoietin-2 with faricimab add beyond VEGF-A blockade?
choices: Stabilization of pericyte-endothelial contacts via Tie2
Laser-like ablation of the peripheral retina
advancedTest.explain: Ang-2 antagonizes Tie2 and destabilizes vessels. Blocking it restores Tie2 signaling.

advancedTest.q: Protocol W found preventive anti-VEGF in severe NPDR reduced progression but did not improve acuity at 4 years. What does this imply?
choices: Severe NPDR rarely progresses to PDR
Anatomic benefit may not translate into visual benefit
Panretinal laser is ineffective in severe NPDR
Anti-VEGF agents have no biological effect in NPDR
advancedTest.explain: The trial separated anatomic outcomes from patient-relevant visual outcomes, which raises the question of whether to treat anatomy alone.

lessons.title: Age-Related Macular Degeneration: Dry and Wet

levels.kid:
At the back of your eye is a thin layer called the retina. It works like the screen in a camera. Right in the middle is a tiny spot called the **macula**. It lets you see small details, like letters in a book or the faces of your friends.

In some older people, the macula slowly wears out. This is called **macular degeneration**. The middle of what they see gets blurry or dark, but the edges still look fine.

There are two kinds. In the **dry** kind, the macula thins out slowly, like an old carpet. In the **wet** kind, leaky new blood vessels grow under it, like a leaky pipe under a floor. Doctors can give eye medicine that stops the leaks. Not smoking and eating green vegetables help protect the macula.
levels.hs:
**Age-related macular degeneration (AMD)** is the leading cause of severe vision loss in people over about 50 in wealthy countries. It damages the **macula**, the small central part of the retina packed with cone cells that give sharp, detailed, color vision. Peripheral (side) vision usually survives, so people rarely go fully blind, but reading, driving and recognizing faces become hard.

AMD affects the **retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)**, a layer of cells that feeds and cleans the light-sensing photoreceptors. Early signs are **drusen**, yellow deposits of waste material under the RPE.

There are two forms:
- **Dry (non-neovascular) AMD**: about 85-90% of cases. Slow thinning and loss of cells. Its late stage is **geographic atrophy**, patches where cells have died.
- **Wet (neovascular) AMD**: about 10-15% of cases but most of the severe vision loss. Abnormal blood vessels grow under the retina, leak fluid and blood, and can cause sudden distortion.

A classic symptom is **metamorphopsia**: straight lines look wavy. Patients can check this at home with an **Amsler grid**, a square grid of lines.

Risk factors include age, smoking (the biggest one you can change), family history and genes. Wet AMD is treated with eye injections that block a growth signal called **VEGF**. For example, a 75-year-old who notices door frames looking bent should be seen urgently, because early treatment saves vision.
levels.college:
AMD is a progressive degeneration of the photoreceptor-RPE-Bruch's membrane-choriocapillaris complex at the macula.

**Pathology**
- **Drusen**: extracellular deposits between the RPE and **Bruch's membrane**, containing lipids, apolipoproteins and complement proteins. Small hard drusen are common with age; large soft drusen and pigment changes signal risk.
- **Reticular pseudodrusen** (subretinal drusenoid deposits) lie above the RPE and also predict progression.
- RPE dysfunction leads to photoreceptor loss.

**Classification (AREDS-based)**
- Early: medium drusen.
- Intermediate: large drusen and/or pigment abnormalities.
- Late: geographic atrophy (dry) or **macular neovascularization (MNV)**, the term now replacing "choroidal neovascularization" (wet).

**Wet AMD mechanism**: hypoxia and inflammation drive RPE secretion of **VEGF-A**, which promotes vessel growth and permeability. New vessels grow from the choroid through Bruch's membrane (type 1 under the RPE, type 2 above it) or arise within the retina (type 3, retinal angiomatous proliferation). Leakage causes fluid, hemorrhage, and eventually a fibrous **disciform scar**.

**Diagnosis**
- **Optical coherence tomography (OCT)**: cross-sectional images showing drusen, intraretinal and subretinal fluid, and RPE detachment. It is the main tool for monitoring.
- **Fluorescein angiography** and **OCT angiography** show the vessels.

**Treatment**
- Intermediate AMD: **AREDS2 supplements** (vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin) reduced progression to late AMD by about 25% over 5 years. Beta-carotene was removed because it raised lung cancer risk in smokers.
- Wet AMD: intravitreal **anti-VEGF** drugs: ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab (off-label), brolucizumab and faricimab.
- Geographic atrophy: complement inhibitors pegcetacoplan (C3) and avacincaptad pegol (C5), approved by the FDA in 2023, slow lesion growth but do not restore vision.
levels.phd:
AMD is a complex disease where aging, oxidative stress, lipid metabolism and innate immunity converge on the RPE-Bruch's membrane interface.

**Genetics.** In 2005, three groups (Klein, Haines and Edwards) found the **complement factor H (CFH) Y402H** variant through one of the first successful genome-wide association studies. It was a landmark for complex-trait genetics. The second major locus is **ARMS2/HTRA1** on chromosome 10q26. The International AMD Genomics Consortium (Fritsche et al., 2016) identified 52 independent variants at 34 loci. These cluster in complement (CFH, C3, C2/CFB, CFI), lipid transport (APOE, CETP, LIPC) and extracellular matrix pathways (TIMP3, COL8A1). Rare CFI loss-of-function variants carry high risk. These loci account for a large share of heritability.

**Mechanism.** Bruch's membrane thickens and accumulates lipid with age, impairing transport between the choriocapillaris and RPE. Drusen contain apolipoproteins, oxidized lipids and complement components. CFH normally regulates the alternative pathway and binds malondialdehyde-modified proteins. The Y402H variant weakens this binding, favoring chronic complement activation, membrane attack complex deposition and inflammasome signaling (NLRP3). Choriocapillaris loss may come before RPE atrophy.

**Anti-VEGF history.** Pegaptanib (2004) was an RNA aptamer against VEGF165 that slowed loss but rarely improved vision. Ranibizumab trials (MARINA, ANCHOR, 2006) showed about 95% of patients kept vision, and roughly a third gained 15 or more letters. This was a turning point in ophthalmology. CATT and IVAN showed bevacizumab was non-inferior to ranibizumab. Aflibercept is a decoy receptor that also binds PlGF. Faricimab adds angiopoietin-2 inhibition, stabilizing vessels via Tie2.

**Controversy.** The complement story is genetically compelling, yet therapeutically modest. Pegcetacoplan (OAKS/DERBY) slowed atrophy growth by roughly 15-20% without a clear functional benefit. Systemic complement inhibition failed entirely. It is unresolved whether complement drives disease or is a downstream amplifier, and whether local or systemic complement matters. ARMS2/HTRA1 biology also remains poorly understood.
levels.expert:
**Clinical realities of anti-VEGF.** Monthly injections in trials give outcomes that fade in the real world under-treatment. Long-term follow-up studies (e.g., SEVEN-UP, 7-year follow-up of ANCHOR/MARINA patients) showed many eyes lost their early gains, often with macular atrophy. Treat-and-extend regimens now dominate. The interval is lengthened when OCT is dry and shortened when fluid recurs. Treatment burden is the central problem. Fluid type matters: intraretinal fluid predicts worse vision, while some subretinal fluid can be tolerated (FLUID trial). Persistent fluid may respond to switching agents.

**Safety pitfalls.** Endophthalmitis is the feared injection complication. Brolucizumab carried a signal of retinal vasculitis and occlusive vasculitis, which limited its use. Pegcetacoplan has been associated with occlusive retinal vasculitis and conversion to exudative AMD. Both are reminders that efficacy signals need real-world surveillance.

**Differentials and phenotypes.** **Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy**, common in Asian populations, needs indocyanine green angiography and may respond to adding photodynamic therapy with verteporfin (EVEREST II). Central serous chorioretinopathy, pachychoroid neovasculopathy, myopic MNV and vitelliform lesions can mimic wet AMD.

**Advances.** Durability strategies include higher-concentration aflibercept formulations, faricimab, and biosimilars that lower cost. The Port Delivery System (refillable ranibizumab implant) had trouble with conjunctival erosion and endophthalmitis. Gene therapies under study include subretinal or suprachoroidal AAV vectors expressing anti-VEGF proteins (e.g., ABBV-RGX-314, ixo-vec), aiming for one-time treatment. Inflammation and dose-response remain issues.

**Imaging biomarkers.** OCT features such as hyperreflective foci, nascent geographic atrophy and drusen volume predict progression. AI analysis of OCT now automates fluid quantification and may personalize intervals. Home OCT monitoring is in trials.

**Open questions.** Can intermediate AMD be halted before atrophy? Cell therapy with RPE patches derived from stem cells (e.g., the London Project, CPCB-RPE1) has shown early feasibility. Photobiomodulation received a contested FDA authorization in 2024 for dry AMD. Patients with low vision should be referred to rehabilitation. Visual hallucinations from vision loss (Charles Bonnet syndrome) should be asked about and normalized.

keyPoints: AMD damages the macula, causing central vision loss while peripheral vision is spared
Drusen under the RPE are the early hallmark
Dry AMD (85-90%) progresses to geographic atrophy; wet AMD causes most severe loss
Wet AMD: VEGF drives macular neovascularization; treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF
OCT is the key imaging tool; Amsler grid detects wavy lines at home
CFH and ARMS2/HTRA1 genes, smoking and age are major risks; AREDS2 slows intermediate AMD

test.q: Which part of vision does AMD mainly destroy?
test.explain: AMD damages the macula, which provides sharp central vision. Peripheral vision is usually preserved.

test.q: What are drusen?
test.explain: Drusen are extracellular deposits between the RPE and Bruch's membrane and are the early sign of AMD.

test.q: Roughly what share of AMD cases are the dry form?
test.explain: Dry AMD makes up most cases, though wet AMD causes most severe vision loss.

test.q: The late stage of dry AMD is called:
test.explain: Geographic atrophy is patchy death of RPE and photoreceptors. A disciform scar is the end stage of wet AMD.

test.q: Which signaling molecule drives vessel growth in wet AMD?
test.explain: VEGF-A promotes new vessel growth and leakiness, and anti-VEGF drugs block it.

test.q: Which imaging test is the main tool for monitoring retinal fluid in AMD?
choices: Plain X-ray of the skull and orbits
Corneal topography of the front eye
test.explain: OCT gives cross-sections showing drusen and intra- or subretinal fluid.

test.q: What is the biggest modifiable risk factor for AMD?
test.explain: Smoking is the main risk factor people can change; age and genes cannot be changed.

test.q: Why was beta-carotene removed from the AREDS2 formula?
choices: It worsened leakage in wet AMD eyes
It caused early cataracts in older adults
It blocked zinc absorption from food
It raised lung cancer risk in smokers
test.explain: Beta-carotene increased lung cancer risk in smokers, so lutein and zeaxanthin replaced it.

test.q: Pegcetacoplan treats geographic atrophy by inhibiting:
test.explain: Pegcetacoplan targets C3 in the complement cascade; avacincaptad pegol targets C5.

test.q: What is the term for straight lines appearing wavy or distorted?
test.explain: Metamorphopsia is a classic symptom of macular disease, especially wet AMD.

test.q: Patients can check for distortion at home using an Amsler ___.
test.explain: The Amsler grid is a square grid of lines that looks wavy or has gaps if the macula is affected.

test.q: Drusen sit between the RPE and ___ membrane.
test.explain: Bruch's membrane separates the RPE from the choriocapillaris.

kidTest.q: What does the macula help you see?
choices: Things in the dark at night
Things far off to the side
kidTest.explain: The macula gives sharp central vision for reading and faces.

kidTest.q: Who usually gets macular degeneration?
kidTest.explain: It happens as people get older.

kidTest.q: What happens in the wet kind?
kidTest.explain: New blood vessels leak under the macula, like a leaky pipe.

kidTest.q: What can help protect the macula?
kidTest.explain: Not smoking and eating green vegetables help.

kidTest.q: The thin layer at the back of the eye is the r _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The retina works like a camera screen.

advancedTest.q: Why was the CFH Y402H discovery important beyond ophthalmology?
choices: It was an early GWAS success for a complex disease
It showed VEGF genes cause dry AMD
It established AMD as a viral disease
It proved AMD is caused by a single gene
advancedTest.explain: The 2005 finding was among the first GWAS successes for a common complex disease, implicating complement.

advancedTest.q: Registry data such as SEVEN-UP showed real-world anti-VEGF results declined mainly because of:
choices: Allergic reactions to the antibody drug
Drug resistance mutations in the vessels
Faulty OCT measurements of retinal fluid
advancedTest.explain: Fewer injections than in trials and developing macular atrophy eroded early gains, driving treat-and-extend strategies.

advancedTest.q: Complement genetics are strong, yet complement drugs give modest benefit. Which is the best reasoning?
choices: Genetic associations prove the drugs target the wrong eye
Complement may amplify damage rather than start it
Complement plays no role in drusen formation
VEGF fully explains dry AMD instead
advancedTest.explain: If complement is a downstream amplifier, or local vs systemic activity matters, inhibition may slow but not stop disease.

advancedTest.q: An Asian patient with wet-AMD-like lesions responds poorly to anti-VEGF. What is the most reasonable next step?
choices: Starting AREDS2 supplements in place of injections
Stopping anti-VEGF treatment as futile for this eye
Indocyanine green angiography to look for polyps
Cataract surgery with lens replacement to improve sight
advancedTest.explain: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy is common in Asian patients, is shown by ICG angiography, and may benefit from added photodynamic therapy.

lessons.title: Retinal Detachment and Retinal Vascular Occlusions

levels.kid:
The **retina** is like the screen at the back of a movie theater, lining the inside of your eye. It catches light and sends pictures to your brain.

Sometimes the screen can peel off the wall. This is called a **retinal detachment**. A person might see lots of new floating specks, flashes of light, or a dark curtain creeping across what they see. That is an emergency, and eye doctors can fix it with surgery.

The retina also needs blood, like a garden needs water from a hose. If a tiny blood pipe gets blocked, part of the retina stops working. This is called an **occlusion**. A sudden, painless loss of sight in one eye means: see a doctor right away!
levels.hs:
The **retina** is the thin, light-sensing layer lining the back of the eye. Two important causes of sudden vision loss involve it.

**Retinal detachment** means the retina separates from the layer beneath it, the **retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)**, which feeds it. The most common type, **rhegmatogenous** detachment, starts with a tear. With age, the jelly filling the eye (the **vitreous**) shrinks and pulls away from the retina. If it tugs hard enough, it rips a hole, and fluid seeps underneath. Warning signs:
- A shower of new **floaters**
- **Photopsia** (flashes of light)
- A shadow or curtain spreading across vision

Nearsighted people, people who have had cataract surgery, and people with eye injuries are at higher risk. Treatment is urgent surgery, especially before the **macula** (the center for sharp vision) detaches.

**Retinal vascular occlusions** are blockages of retinal blood vessels:
- **Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)** causes sudden, painless, severe vision loss. It is basically a stroke of the eye, often from an embolus (a traveling clot) coming from the carotid artery or the heart.
- **Retinal vein occlusion** causes bleeding and swelling, so the retina looks like a 'blood and thunder' picture.

Example: a 68-year-old with high blood pressure who suddenly goes blind in one eye needs emergency stroke evaluation, not just eye care.
levels.college:
**Retinal detachment (RD)** is separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE. Photoreceptors depend on the RPE and choroid for oxygen, so detached retina degenerates over days. There are three mechanisms:
- **Rhegmatogenous**: a full-thickness break lets liquefied vitreous enter the subretinal space. This is the most common type. It usually follows **posterior vitreous detachment (PVD)**, with traction at sites of strong vitreoretinal adhesion. Horseshoe tears are typical. Risk factors include high myopia, lattice degeneration, previous cataract surgery, trauma and RD in the other eye.
- **Tractional**: fibrovascular membranes pull the retina off without a break, as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
- **Exudative (serous)**: fluid leaks under an intact retina, from tumors, inflammation or severe hypertension.

Symptomatic PVD needs a **dilated fundus exam** with scleral depression. Pigment cells in the vitreous ('tobacco dust', or **Shafer sign**) strongly suggest a tear. Tears without detachment are sealed with **laser retinopexy** or cryotherapy. Detachments are repaired by:
- **Pneumatic retinopexy** (a gas bubble plus freezing or laser)
- **Scleral buckle** (an external band that pushes the eye wall toward the retina)
- **Pars plana vitrectomy** with gas or silicone oil tamponade

The key prognostic factor is whether the **macula** is still attached ('mac-on' versus 'mac-off').

**CRAO** produces a pale, swollen retina with a **cherry-red spot**: the fovea has no inner retina, so the normal choroid shows through. Emboli may be visible as bright **Hollenhorst plaques** (cholesterol). In patients over 50, giant cell arteritis must be excluded with ESR, CRP and urgent steroids. **Branch** occlusions affect a sector of the retina.

**Retinal vein occlusion (RVO)**, central or branch, is linked to hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma and age. The fundus shows flame hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins and cotton-wool spots. The major causes of vision loss are **macular edema**, treated with anti-VEGF injections, and ischemic neovascularization, treated with laser.
levels.phd:
The neurosensory retina adheres to the RPE without junctions. Adhesion depends on interdigitation of RPE microvilli with photoreceptor outer segments, the interphotoreceptor matrix, and active RPE pumping of fluid toward the choroid. Na+/K+-ATPase and water transport through aquaporins generate a net outward flow. For a rhegmatogenous RD to form, there must be a break, liquefied vitreous, and traction (or fluid currents) that overwhelm these forces. Age-related vitreous liquefaction (**synchysis**) and collapse (**syneresis**) produce PVD. Firm adhesion at the vitreous base, retinal vessels and lattice borders concentrates traction there. That explains why horseshoe tears sit near the vitreous base, with their flap attached anteriorly.

After detachment, photoreceptors begin apoptosis within hours. Outer segments shorten, Müller glia proliferate, and rod-cone remodeling follows. Outcome depends on the duration of foveal detachment, which is why mac-off repair is commonly done within days. The main cause of failed surgery is **proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR)**. In PVR, RPE cells undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and, together with glia and macrophages, form contractile membranes driven by TGF-β and PDGF signaling.

The inner retina is supplied by the central retinal artery, an end-artery branch of the ophthalmic artery. The outer retina is supplied by the choroid. About 15-30% of eyes have a **cilioretinal artery** from the choroidal circulation, which can preserve central vision during CRAO. Primate experiments by Hayreh suggested the retina tolerates roughly 90-100 minutes of complete ischemia before irreversible damage, although later analyses dispute how this applies to humans with incomplete occlusion.

Vein occlusions often occur where an artery crosses a vein. At these crossings the two share an adventitial sheath, so arteriosclerotic compression causes turbulence and thrombosis; at the optic disc, the lamina cribrosa plays a similar role. Ischemia drives HIF-1α and VEGF upregulation, which breaks down the blood-retinal barrier (causing edema) and promotes neovascularization. The Central Vein Occlusion Study defined ischemic CRVO as 10 or more disc areas of nonperfusion, which predicts iris neovascularization and **neovascular glaucoma** (the '100-day glaucoma').
levels.expert:
Sudden painless monocular vision loss from CRAO is now managed as an **acute ischemic stroke**. Silent brain infarcts appear on diffusion-weighted MRI in roughly a quarter of patients, and stroke risk is highest in the first weeks. AHA guidance supports immediate referral to a stroke center for carotid imaging, cardiac rhythm monitoring and echocardiography. Older 'conservative' maneuvers, such as ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis and lowering eye pressure, failed to beat natural history and have largely been abandoned. The EAGLE trial found that intra-arterial fibrinolysis was no better than conservative care and caused more adverse events. Intravenous thrombolysis within about 4.5 hours shows promise in pooled observational data, and randomized trials (THEIA, REVISION, TenCRAOS) are testing it. In anyone over 50, think of **giant cell arteritis** first: jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, a chalky-white disc or choroidal hypoperfusion make steroids an emergency.

For RVO, the SCORE2, BRAVO/CRUISE and COPERNICUS/GALILEO trials made **anti-VEGF agents** (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) first-line for macular edema. Dexamethasone implants are a second-line option but raise eye pressure and cause cataract. Systemic workup focuses on blood pressure, diabetes, lipids and glaucoma; thrombophilia screening is reserved for young or bilateral cases. OCT angiography now maps nonperfusion without dye.

In RD, the PIVOT trial showed that pneumatic retinopexy gave better vision and less metamorphopsia than vitrectomy for eligible detachments. Pneumatic repair, however, needs strict head positioning, and patients with gas in the eye must avoid air travel and nitrous oxide anesthesia, which can expand the bubble dangerously. Scleral buckling remains favored in young phakic patients with attached vitreous. Vitrectomy dominates in pseudophakic eyes and complex cases.

Pitfalls:
- Missing a tear because the exam was undilated or the periphery was not depressed
- Reassuring a patient with vitreous hemorrhage without ultrasound, when hemorrhage can hide a tear
- Calling flashes 'migraine' in a myopic patient

Open questions: no proven pharmacologic prevention of PVR exists (methotrexate is under study, as in the GUARD trial); neuroprotection after retinal ischemia is unproven; and the true time window for reperfusion in humans is still uncertain.

keyPoints: Retinal detachment separates the neurosensory retina from the RPE
Rhegmatogenous RD follows a tear, usually after posterior vitreous detachment
Floaters, flashes and a curtain over vision are warning signs
Macula-on versus macula-off status drives urgency and prognosis
CRAO causes a cherry-red spot and is treated as a stroke; exclude giant cell arteritis
Vein occlusion causes hemorrhages and macular edema treated with anti-VEGF

test.q: The most common type of retinal detachment begins with:
test.explain: Rhegmatogenous RD starts with a tear that lets liquefied vitreous enter the subretinal space. Tumor leakage causes exudative RD, and membranes cause tractional RD.

test.q: Which symptom set suggests a retinal tear or detachment?
test.explain: New floaters, photopsia and a spreading shadow are the classic warning triad. Halos with pain and vomiting suggest acute angle-closure glaucoma instead.

test.q: Tractional retinal detachment is classically associated with:
test.explain: Fibrovascular membranes in proliferative diabetic retinopathy pull the retina off without a break.

test.q: Why does CRAO produce a cherry-red spot?
choices: The fovea lacks swollen inner retina
test.explain: The fovea has no inner retinal layers, so the normal choroid shows through while the surrounding ischemic retina turns pale.

test.q: In a 75-year-old with CRAO and jaw claudication, which test is urgent?
test.explain: Giant cell arteritis must be excluded with ESR and CRP and treated urgently with steroids.

test.q: The 'blood and thunder' fundus appearance describes:
test.explain: Widespread hemorrhages and dilated, tortuous veins characterize CRVO. CRAO produces a pale retina instead.

test.q: First-line treatment for macular edema from vein occlusion is:
test.explain: Anti-VEGF agents reduce the leakage driven by ischemia-induced VEGF. Retinopexy seals tears, which is a different problem.

test.q: The most important prognostic factor in retinal detachment is:
test.explain: Mac-on detachments keep good central vision if repaired promptly. Mac-off eyes have a poorer outcome.

test.q: Bright cholesterol emboli seen in retinal arterioles are called:
test.explain: Hollenhorst plaques are cholesterol emboli, often coming from the carotid artery.

test.q: Age-related separation of the vitreous gel from the retina is called posterior vitreous ___.
test.explain: PVD is the usual trigger for horseshoe retinal tears.

test.q: What is the term for flashes of light seen when the vitreous tugs on the retina?
test.explain: Photopsia comes from mechanical stimulation of the retina by vitreous traction.

test.q: Which surgery places an external band on the eye wall to repair a detachment?
test.explain: A scleral buckle indents the eye wall toward the detached retina, closing the break.

kidTest.q: What does the retina do?
choices: Makes tears to wash the eye
Moves the eye left and right
kidTest.explain: The retina is like a movie screen at the back of the eye.

kidTest.q: What is a retinal detachment?
kidTest.explain: The retina comes away from the wall behind it.

kidTest.q: Which sign could mean the retina is detaching?
kidTest.explain: A spreading shadow, flashes and new floaters are warning signs.

kidTest.q: What should someone do if they suddenly lose sight in one eye?
kidTest.explain: Sudden vision loss is an emergency.

kidTest.q: A blocked blood pipe in the retina is called an o _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: An occlusion is a blockage that stops blood from reaching part of the retina.

advancedTest.q: A patient with CRAO keeps good central vision. The best explanation is:
choices: The embolus lodged in a vortex vein draining the choroid
A cilioretinal artery from the choroidal circulation perfuses the macula
Photoreceptors survive ischemia because they lack mitochondria
The fovea is fed directly by the central retinal artery
advancedTest.explain: A cilioretinal artery (present in about 15-30% of eyes) can supply the macula independently of the occluded central retinal artery.

advancedTest.q: Why has CRAO care shifted toward stroke-center referral?
choices: CRAO signals cerebrovascular disease with high early stroke risk
Retinal ischemia is reversible for many hours in most patients
Ocular massage was shown to reliably restore lost vision
Intra-arterial fibrinolysis clearly outperformed conservative care
advancedTest.explain: Silent brain infarcts and early stroke risk make CRAO a stroke equivalent. EAGLE showed no benefit from intra-arterial fibrinolysis.

advancedTest.q: Why do branch vein occlusions arise at arteriovenous crossings?
choices: Veins carry higher pressure there than the arteries
A shared adventitial sheath lets stiff arteries compress the vein
The RPE pump draws blood out of the vein at crossings
Müller glia secrete clotting factors at vessel crossings
advancedTest.explain: Arteriosclerotic compression within the common sheath creates turbulence, endothelial damage and thrombosis.

advancedTest.q: A redetachment weeks after repair, with stiff retinal folds, most likely reflects:
choices: Choroidal tumor leakage producing new serous fluid
Vitreous synchysis occurring for the first time
Excess aquaporin activity pumping fluid out of the subretinal space
Contractile membranes formed after RPE epithelial-mesenchymal transition
advancedTest.explain: This is proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR): RPE and glial cells form contractile membranes driven by TGF-β and PDGF, and it is the main cause of surgical failure.
